info.desc: Rage Against the Machine is the debut album by rock band Rage Against the Machine, released November 3, 1992. The songs on Rage Against the Machine tend to feature political mantras with the vocals rapped. The album peaked at #1 on Billboard's Heatseekers chart, and at #45 on the Billboard Top 200 chart. Tom Morello's guitar soloing is somewhat traditional on this album, taking influence more from heavy metal music, in comparison to later releases where it is more experimental and geared toward emulation of DJs and hip hop. In 2001 Q magazine named Rage Against the Machine as one .

podcast.body: Released in the early 1990s, this album represented a revolutionary shift in rock music, contrasting sharply with the introspective themes prevalent in Grunge and the generally less content-rich rock of the 1980s. It introduced a radical new style, substance, and form to the musical landscape. "Al final Richa Gance Machine salía a primerísimo solo los 90, cuando en el mercado musical del rock, yo creo que estábamos yendo a otro camino, porque estábamos en pleno a ojo de la música Grunge."

podcast.body: The back cover of the album's booklet featured an image of a dollar bill with the phrase "no eres un esclavo, Joan of the Slayf" written on it. This potent anti-slavery message later became an influential motif, referenced by bands like System of a Down. "El detalle más genial de rechagan semacín dentro de ese disco que lo abrías y la contraportada del libretto era la imagen de un billete de un dólar que tenía escrito no eres un esclavo, Joan of the Slayf."

podcast.body: The band's powerful debut record, released in 1992, was produced by Canadian Garth Richardson. To capture a live sound, Richardson set up the band in a large room, routed all their audio into a concert PA system, and then mic'd those speakers, instructing the band to play. This recording method is credited with contributing to the album's distinct live feel. "He set the band up in a big room and routed all their audio into a concert PA system. He then mic those speakers and told them to play."

podcast.title: Debut Album
podcast.body: Released on November 3rd, 1992, this album features a powerful photograph of Thich Kwan Duk, a burning Buddhist monk, on its cover. The liner notes clearly state, "no samples, keyboards or synthesizers were used in the making of this record." The album includes guest vocals from Maynard James Keenan of Tool and Stephen Perkins of Jane's Addiction. Notably, the version of "Bullet in the Head" on the album was recorded before the band had ever performed live. Renowned for its audio quality, "Track 3, take the power back" is specifically recommended for testing speakers and amplifiers. "on November 3rd, 1992, the album with a dying, Fitchquan dock on the cover appeared in stores."

podcast.body: This self-titled video concert album, released on VHS, notably included a very loud cover version of Bruce Springsteen's "The Ghost of Tom Joad." The studio version of this cover was presented as the first full song on the tape. "In 1997, Rage released a self-titled video concert album on VHS that included a very loud cover of the song."
